cues.text: A complex number can be represented as an ordered pair of real numbers a, b,
or
written a plus i b, where i squared equals negative one.
Its real part is a and its imaginary part is b, not i b.
Equality means both corresponding real components agree.
Addition and subtraction operate component by component.
Multiplication follows distribution together with i squared equals negative
one.
For example, two plus three i times one minus i equals two minus two i plus
three i minus three i squared.
Replacing i squared by negative one gives five plus i.
Powers of i repeat every four steps: i, negative one, negative i, one.
Divide an integer exponent by four and use its remainder.
Twenty three leaves remainder three, so i to the power twenty three is
negative
i.
For negative exponents, use reciprocals or extend the same four step cycle.
A complex number is real exactly when its imaginary part is zero, and is
purely
imaginary with nonzero imaginary component when its real part is zero.
Do not apply ordinary greater than comparisons to arbitrary complex numbers.
Algebraic equality and modulus comparisons are meaningful, but there is no
usual real ordering compatible with complex arithmetic.
The conjugate of a plus i b is a minus i b.
Their product is a squared plus b squared, a nonnegative real number.
Its square root is the modulus, the distance of the point from the origin.
Thus three plus four i has modulus five and conjugate three minus four i.
Conjugation respects addition and multiplication, while the modulus of a
product equals the product of the moduli.
To divide by a nonzero complex number, multiply numerator and denominator by
the conjugate of the denominator.
For three plus four i divided by one minus two i, multiply by one plus two i.
The numerator becomes negative five plus ten i, and the denominator becomes
five.
The quotient is negative one plus two i.
Check by multiplying that quotient by one minus two i to recover three plus
four i.
The reciprocal formula uses the conjugate divided by modulus squared, not
divided by the modulus alone.
If the denominator is zero, the formula is unavailable.
Also, the modulus of a sum is at most the sum of the moduli, not generally
equal to it.
For one plus i and one minus i, the sum has modulus two, while the individual
moduli add to two square root of two.
In the Argand plane, a complex number a plus i b is the point with horizontal
coordinate a and vertical coordinate b.
This connects algebra to geometry.
The modulus of z minus a fixed complex number z zero is the ordinary distance
between their points.
Consequently, modulus of z minus two equals three describes a circle centred
at
two, zero with radius three.
It does not mean that the modulus of z is one.
Squaring the nonnegative distance equation gives x minus two squared plus y
squared equals nine when z is x plus i y.
Equal distances from two fixed points describe their perpendicular bisector.
For example, modulus of z minus one equals modulus of z plus one compares
distances from one, zero and negative one, zero.
Squaring and simplifying gives x equal to zero, the imaginary axis.
Conjugation reflects a point across the real axis, while negation reflects it
through the origin.
Addition combines coordinate displacements.
A modulus cannot be negative, so an equation asking a modulus to equal a
negative real number has no solution.
Keep the complex variable and its real coordinate components distinct while
translating a geometric condition into algebra.
For a nonzero complex number, an argument is the angle its position vector
makes with the positive real axis.
Angles differing by an integer multiple of two pi describe the same direction.
We use the principal interval greater than negative pi and at most pi in this
class.
Always state the convention because another text may use a different endpoint
convention.
The point negative one plus i lies in quadrant two, has modulus square root of
two, and principal argument three pi over four.
Using only inverse tangent of imaginary part divided by real part would
suggest
negative pi over four and miss the quadrant.
In polar form, write z as r times cosine theta plus i sine theta, with
positive
r equal to the modulus.
Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments; division by a nonzero
number divides moduli and subtracts arguments.
Reduce the angle to the chosen principal interval only after the operation.
For example, i times i has modulus one and angle pi, giving negative one.
The zero complex number has modulus zero but no defined direction, so its
argument is undefined.
Argument is also not additive across sums: determine the sum's coordinates
before assigning its direction.
A quadratic equation has the form a z squared plus b z plus c equals zero with
a nonzero.
Completing the square gives the quadratic formula.
For real coefficients, the discriminant b squared minus four a c classifies
the roots.
A positive value gives two distinct real roots; zero gives one repeated real
root; a negative value gives two nonreal complex conjugate roots.
For z squared minus two z plus five equals zero, the discriminant is negative
sixteen.
Its square roots are plus or minus four i, giving roots one plus two i and one
minus two i.
Substitute either root to check.
Complex square roots can also be found by setting the square root equal to u
plus i v and comparing real and imaginary parts after squaring.
For three plus four i, equations u squared minus v squared equals three and
two
u v equals four are satisfied by u equal to two and v equal to one.
Thus the two square roots are two plus i and negative two minus i.
They are opposites, not complex conjugates of one another.
Squaring is the final check, and a nonzero complex number has two square roots
with opposite signs.
When a coefficient contains a parameter, begin by checking whether the
equation
remains quadratic.
Then compute the discriminant with the signs of all coefficients included.
Consider x squared minus two k x plus k plus two equals zero.
Its leading coefficient is one for every real k.
The discriminant is four k squared minus four k minus eight, which factors as
four times k minus two times k plus one.
Real roots require this expression to be nonnegative.
Mark negative one and two on the parameter line.
The two factors have the same sign outside the interval between them, so real
roots occur for k at most negative one or k at least two.
At either endpoint the root is repeated.
For k between those values the roots are nonreal complex conjugates.
Do not infer the interval from just one factor, and do not forget equality
when
the question permits repeated roots.
As a separate warning, in k minus one times x squared plus two x plus one
equals zero, k equal to one removes the squared term.
That case is linear and must be solved directly.
A discriminant formula derived under a nonzero leading coefficient cannot
replace this separate check.
Let alpha and beta be the roots of a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero,
where a is nonzero.
Expanding a times x minus alpha times x minus beta and comparing coefficients
gives alpha plus beta equal to negative b over a, and alpha beta equal to c
over a.
These identities hold whether roots are real, repeated or nonreal complex.
They are often more efficient than solving for each root.
For two x squared minus five x plus two equals zero, the sum is five halves
and
the product is one.
The sum of their squares is the square of five halves minus twice one, giving
seventeen quarters.
The square of a sum includes a cross term, so it is not the same as the sum of
squares.
The sum of reciprocals is the root sum divided by the root product, provided
neither root is zero.
Here it is five halves.
Higher symmetric expressions can be reduced using the same sum and product.
For example, the sum of cubes equals the cube of the sum minus three times the
product times the sum.
Before dividing by the product, check c is nonzero; otherwise at least one
root
is zero and reciprocal expressions are undefined.
To form a monic quadratic from two roots, calculate their sum S and product P,
then write x squared minus S x plus P equals zero.
Multiplying the whole equation by a nonzero constant gives the same roots.
Starting from roots two and three, the sum is five and product is six, so the
equation is x squared minus five x plus six equals zero.
If the new roots are one more than each original root, they are three and
four.
Their sum is seven and product twelve, giving x squared minus seven x plus
twelve equals zero.
More generally, shifting both roots by h changes the sum to S plus two h and
product to P plus h S plus h squared.
Reciprocal roots have sum S divided by P and product one divided by P,
requiring P nonzero.
For roots two and three, multiply the monic reciprocal equation by six to
obtain six x squared minus five x plus one equals zero.
A real coefficient quadratic with a nonreal root must also have its conjugate
as the other root.
Thus a root one plus two i gives the companion one minus two i and equation x
squared minus two x plus five equals zero.
Two equations sharing a root must both vanish at the same input.
Subtracting them can simplify the search, but any candidate must still satisfy
the originals.
Compare x squared minus three x plus two equals zero and x squared minus k x
plus two equals zero.
Subtracting gives three minus k times x equals zero.
The first polynomial has roots one and two, so the common root cannot be zero.
Therefore k equals three.
At that value the two polynomials coincide and share both roots.
If you divided by x without first excluding zero, the reasoning would have
missed a possible case in another problem.
Degree changes deserve the same care.
For k minus one times x squared plus two x plus one equals zero, k equal to
one
gives the linear equation two x plus one equals zero, whose solution is
negative one half.
For k not equal to one the equation is quadratic, and its discriminant is four
times two minus k.
At k equal to two there is a repeated root negative one; for k greater than
two
there are no real roots.
Parameter conclusions must retain the exceptional linear case instead of
silently dividing by zero.
A root location question needs more than a positive product.
First ensure real roots, then combine their sum and product with the desired
boundary.
For x squared minus six x plus k equals zero, ask when both roots are strictly
greater than one, allowing a repeated root.
Set x equal to t plus one so the condition becomes both t roots positive.
The transformed equation is t squared minus four t plus k minus five equals
zero.
Its root sum is four, already positive.
For real roots with a positive sum, a positive product forces both to be
positive; a negative product would put them on opposite sides of zero.
Thus require k greater than five.
Reality of the roots requires the original discriminant thirty six minus four
k
to be nonnegative, so k is at most nine.
Combining gives k greater than five and at most nine.
At k equal to five, one original root is exactly one and fails the strict
condition.
At k equal to nine, both roots equal three and qualify.
Finally, for an upward opening quadratic with real roots two and three, the
expression is nonpositive between those roots and positive outside.
Mark endpoints according to whether equality is permitted.
